questions.question: A 225 g mass is rotating at 75 revolutions per minute on a 4.0 m long string. How would the angular velocity of this mass change if it continued to rotate with the same frequency, but the string was let out until it was 6.0 m long?
questions.answer: $\omega=2\pi f$ depends only on frequency, which is unchanged.
options: The angular velocity would be 1.5 times greater.
The angular velocity would decrease by one third.
The angular velocity would decrease by two thirds.
The angular velocity would not change.

questions.question: Which identifies the characteristics of the motion of a projectile?
questions.answer: Without air resistance the only force is gravity, so horizontal velocity is constant and vertical acceleration is uniform.
options: The vertical velocity is greater than the horizontal velocity.
Both the net velocity and acceleration are constant.
It has constant horizontal motion and uniformly accelerated vertical motion.
It has constant vertical motion and uniformly accelerated horizontal motion.

questions.question: Three current-carrying wires are set up as shown. The force on wire Y due to the other two wires is $F$. What will happen to the force on Y if the currents in X and Z are each doubled but the distances stay the same?
questions.answer: Each force on Y is proportional to the other wire's current, so both double (they oppose each other) and the resultant doubles.
options: It will be the same value but in the opposite direction.

questions.question: Atom X undergoes alpha decay to form atom Y. How will the nucleus of Y be different from that of X?
questions.answer: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
options: The nucleus of Y will have 2 more protons than X.
The nucleus of Y will have 2 fewer protons but the same number of neutrons as X.
The nucleus of Y will have 2 more protons and 2 more neutrons than X.
The nucleus of Y will have 2 fewer protons and 2 fewer neutrons than X.

questions.question: The figure shows a vehicle travelling in a horizontal circle at constant speed on a frictionless banked track. Which arrow, A, B, C or D, represents the direction of the net force on the vehicle?
questions.answer: The net force is centripetal: horizontal, towards the centre of the circle.

questions.question: A laptop charger (transformer) with 1600 turns in the primary coil and 800 turns in the secondary coil supplies a current of 3.34 A from its secondary. If the transformer is ideal, what is the current in the primary coil?
questions.answer: $I_p=I_s\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}=3.34\times\dfrac{800}{1600}=1.67$ A.

questions.question: The absorption spectra of four metals and a star are shown. Which metals are present in the star?
questions.answer: All the star's lines are accounted for by the calcium and iron lines; the sodium and magnesium lines do not all match.

questions.question: The experiment shown demonstrates the photoelectric effect. Light of a fixed frequency is directed onto a metal plate and the photocurrent is measured with the ammeter. If the intensity of the light is increased, what else will increase?
questions.answer: Greater intensity means more photons per second, so more photoelectrons per second.

questions.question: A charged particle $q$ enters a uniform magnetic field $B$ with velocity $v$ and follows a circular path of radius $r$ as shown. If the magnitude of the field was doubled with other variables constant, what would the new radius be?
questions.answer: $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}\propto\dfrac1B$.

questions.question: “Prior to digital technology, the use of a pendulum was the most accurate method for determining the acceleration due to gravity in a school laboratory.” Which explanation best justifies this statement?
questions.answer: Timing many swings greatly reduces the error in the period, and the length can be measured precisely.
options: Pendulums are very easy for students to set up.
The equations needed for calculations are easy to use.
Measurement errors for the main variables can be minimised.
A stop watch can be used to measure the time for one swing.

questions.question: A cannon fires a projectile from a cliff with an initial velocity of 110 m s$^{-1}$ at $55^\circ$ above the horizontal. The muzzle is 1.5 m above the top of a 52 m cliff (diagram not to scale; ignore air resistance). What is the maximum height above ground level reached by the projectile?
questions.answer:
$u_y=110\sin55^\circ=90.1$ m s$^{-1}$. At maximum height $v_y=0$:
$$\Delta y=\frac{u_y^2}{2g}=\frac{90.1^2}{19.6}=414\text{ m}$$
Height above ground $=414+53.5\approx468$ m.

questions.question: A cannon fires a projectile from a cliff with an initial velocity of 110 m s$^{-1}$ at $55^\circ$ above the horizontal. The muzzle is 1.5 m above the top of a 52 m cliff (diagram not to scale; ignore air resistance). What is the velocity of the projectile at maximum height?
questions.answer: $v=u_x=110\cos55^\circ=63.1$ m s$^{-1}$, horizontally.

questions.question: A cannon fires a projectile from a cliff with an initial velocity of 110 m s$^{-1}$ at $55^\circ$ above the horizontal. The muzzle is 1.5 m above the top of a 52 m cliff (diagram not to scale; ignore air resistance). How far has the projectile travelled horizontally when it reaches maximum height?

The table gives data for the 8 planets of the solar system. The mass of the Sun is $2.00\times10^{30}$ kg. At what distance from the Sun is Mercury travelling with its greatest orbital speed? Which of Kepler's laws did you use?
questions.answer: At perihelion, $46\times10^6$ km. Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times): the planet moves fastest when closest to the Sun.

questions.question: The table gives data for the 8 planets of the solar system. The mass of the Sun is $2.00\times10^{30}$ kg. What is the average gravitational force between the Sun and Mars?
The table gives data for the 8 planets of the solar system. The mass of the Sun is $2.00\times10^{30}$ kg. What is the gravitational field strength at the surface of Saturn?

questions.answer: $$v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times6.67\times10^{-11}\times568\times10^{24}}{6.027\times10^7}}=3.55\times10^4\text{ m s}^{-1}$$

questions.question: Students investigated the relationship between radius and speed for a 42 g mass in uniform circular motion. The centripetal force was kept constant for each radius, and the time for 10 complete cycles was measured (table). They were asked to use all the results to determine the magnitude of the constant centripetal force. List and explain the steps of the analysis required (you are not required to calculate the force).
questions.answer:
1. Convert each radius to metres and the mass to kilograms (0.042 kg) so the force is in newtons.
2. Divide each time by 10 to get the period $T$ (timing 10 cycles reduces timing error).
3. Calculate each speed: $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$.
4. Since $F=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ with $F$ constant, $v^2=\dfrac{F}{m}r$. Calculate $v^2$ for each trial and plot $v^2$ (vertical) against $r$ (horizontal).
5. Draw a line of best fit through the origin and find its gradient, which equals $F/m$.
6. Calculate $F=m\times\text{gradient}$. The line of best fit uses all the data and reduces the effect of random errors.

questions.question: A motor uses a coil of 80 turns measuring 0.092 m (side AB) by 0.077 m. A current of 1.5 A flows in the direction shown. The coil is vertical, in a magnetic field of $5.1\times10^{-2}$ T directed upwards. What are the magnitude and direction of the magnetic force on side AB?
questions.answer: $$F=nBIl=80\times5.1\times10^{-2}\times1.5\times0.092=0.56\text{ N}$$Direction: out of the page (current to the right, field up).

questions.question: A motor uses a coil of 80 turns measuring 0.092 m (side AB) by 0.077 m. A current of 1.5 A flows in the direction shown. The coil is vertical, in a magnetic field of $5.1\times10^{-2}$ T directed upwards. What are the magnitude and direction of the torque on the coil in this position?
questions.answer: $$\tau=nBIA\sin\theta=80\times5.1\times10^{-2}\times1.5\times(0.092\times0.077)\times\sin90^\circ=4.3\times10^{-2}\text{ N m}$$Side AB is pushed out of the page and CD into the page, so the coil rotates clockwise when viewed from the left-hand end of the axle.

questions.question: A motor uses a coil of 80 turns measuring 0.092 m (side AB) by 0.077 m. A current of 1.5 A flows in the direction shown. The coil is vertical, in a magnetic field of $5.1\times10^{-2}$ T directed upwards. The coil rotates as a result of the torque. What happens to the magnitude of the torque as the coil rotates through $90^\circ$?
questions.answer: It decreases from its maximum to zero, varying with the cosine of the angle rotated, as the plane of the coil becomes perpendicular to the field.

questions.question: A rectangular loop of wire is moved at constant velocity across a magnetic field, with its plane always perpendicular to the field. While entering the field (Fig. 1) a current flows in the direction shown and the loop experiences a force opposite to its motion. When the loop is entirely inside the field (Fig. 2) there is no current and no opposing force. Use Faraday's and Lenz's laws to explain this.
questions.answer:
**Faraday:** an emf is induced when the magnetic flux through the loop changes, with magnitude equal to the rate of change of flux.
**Fig. 1:** as the loop enters, the area inside the field increases, so the flux into the page increases. An emf is induced and, the loop being closed, a current flows.
**Lenz:** the current is in the direction that opposes the change: anticlockwise, producing flux out of the page inside the loop. The motor-effect force on the leading side (inside the field) therefore acts opposite to the motion. Work done against this force supplies the electrical energy (conservation of energy).
**Fig. 2:** the whole loop is in a uniform field, so the flux stays constant while it moves. There is no induced emf, no current and hence no opposing force.

questions.question: A battery-operated electric drill was connected to an ammeter to measure the current in the rotor. When switched on, the current rapidly rose to 5.5 A and then quickly fell to a steady 0.9 A. When used to drill a hole (a load on the motor), the current rose to 2.1 A, as shown. Explain why the current changed like this.
questions.answer:
The current is set by the net voltage across the rotor: $I=\dfrac{V_{supply}-\varepsilon_{back}}{R}$.
- **Start-up:** the rotor is stationary, so there is no back emf. The full supply voltage acts across the small coil resistance, giving a large current (5.5 A).
- **Speeding up:** the motor effect turns the rotor. The rotating coils experience changing flux, inducing a back emf that by Lenz's law opposes the supply. It grows with speed, so the current falls.
- **Steady running:** at constant speed the back emf is constant and nearly equals the supply voltage; the small current (0.9 A) only provides enough torque to overcome friction.
- **Drilling:** the load slows the rotor, reducing the back emf. The net voltage and current rise (2.1 A), giving the extra torque needed to do work on the load.

questions.question: During the 1700s Newton and Huygens proposed very different hypotheses on the nature of light. Compare Newton's and Huygens' models of light, including ONE similarity and ONE difference.
questions.answer:
**Newton (corpuscular):** light consists of streams of tiny, perfectly elastic particles (corpuscles) travelling in straight lines.
**Huygens (wave):** light is a (longitudinal) wave propagating through a medium, the aether; each point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets.
**Similarity:** both could explain reflection and refraction.
**Difference:** particles versus waves. Consequently Newton predicted light travels faster in a denser medium, whereas Huygens predicted it travels slower; Huygens' model could also account for diffraction.

questions.question: Huygens' model of light was accepted over Newton's largely due to the experimental work of Thomas Young. What did Young's work show and how did it support Huygens over Newton?
questions.answer: Young's double-slit experiment produced alternating bright and dark fringes from light passing through two slits: interference. Constructive and destructive interference is a property of waves and cannot be explained by particles, supporting Huygens' wave model.

questions.question: Photoelectric effect data for a sodium target are given in the table (frequency in $10^{14}$ Hz: 6.0, 8.8, 12.5, 15.0, 16.4; maximum electron kinetic energy in eV: 0.18, 1.32, 2.85, 3.81, 4.65). Plot a graph of maximum electron kinetic energy against frequency and draw a line of best fit, extending it to the vertical axis.
questions.answer: The points lie close to a straight line with horizontal intercept (threshold frequency) about $5.6\times10^{14}$ Hz and vertical intercept about $-2.4$ eV (graph).

questions.question: Photoelectric effect data for a sodium target are given in the table (frequency in $10^{14}$ Hz: 6.0, 8.8, 12.5, 15.0, 16.4; maximum electron kinetic energy in eV: 0.18, 1.32, 2.85, 3.81, 4.65). Use a line of best fit to derive a value for Planck's constant in eV s.
questions.answer: $K_{max}=hf-\phi$, so $h$ is the gradient:$$h=\frac{\Delta K}{\Delta f}\approx\frac{4.2\text{ eV}}{10\times10^{14}\text{ Hz}}\approx4.2\times10^{-15}\text{ eV s}$$

questions.question: Photoelectric effect data for a sodium target are given in the table (frequency in $10^{14}$ Hz: 6.0, 8.8, 12.5, 15.0, 16.4; maximum electron kinetic energy in eV: 0.18, 1.32, 2.85, 3.81, 4.65). Find the work function of sodium from the line of best fit.
questions.answer: The vertical intercept is $-\phi$, giving $\phi\approx2.4$ eV.

questions.question: An oil drop of mass $1.177\times10^{-15}$ kg falls into the evacuated space between two parallel charged plates 2.00 cm apart. The drop is negatively charged. The voltage is adjusted until the drop is stationary, at a potential difference of 72.0 V. How many excess electrons are on the drop?
Robert Millikan used an experiment in which charged oil drops were held between parallel plates. What did he conclude from his investigation?
questions.answer: Charge is quantised: every drop's charge was an integer multiple of a basic charge, the charge of the electron (about $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C).

questions.question: The diagram represents a hydrogen atom with transitions between energy levels $n=1$ to $6$. The atom absorbs a photon causing an electron to move from level 2 to level 5 (transition A). What is the frequency of the absorbed photon?
questions.answer: $$\frac1\lambda=R\left(\frac1{2^2}-\frac1{5^2}\right)=1.097\times10^7\times0.21,\quad\lambda=434\text{ nm}$$$$f=\frac c\lambda=\frac{3.00\times10^8}{4.34\times10^{-7}}=6.91\times10^{14}\text{ Hz}$$

questions.question: The diagram represents a hydrogen atom with transitions between energy levels $n=1$ to $6$. What results from the electron transition marked F, from level 4 to level 1? (No calculation required.)
questions.answer: Emission of a single photon of ultraviolet radiation (Lyman series).

questions.question: Our understanding of the atom changed significantly between 1904 and 1913 through the contributions of Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr. Outline the main features of each model and explain how each model improved upon the existing model.
questions.answer:
**Thomson (1904):** having discovered the electron (1897, from its charge-to-mass ratio in cathode ray experiments), he proposed the "plum pudding" model: a sphere of uniformly spread positive charge with electrons embedded in it, neutral overall.
*Improvement:* replaced the indivisible atom (Dalton) with an atom that has internal structure and contains electrons.

**Rutherford (1911):** based on the Geiger–Marsden alpha-scattering experiment, in which most alpha particles passed through gold foil but a few deflected through large angles. The atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus containing nearly all its mass, and electrons orbiting it.
*Improvement:* explained large-angle scattering, which diffuse positive charge could not.
*Limitations:* orbiting (accelerating) electrons should radiate and spiral into the nucleus; it could not explain line spectra.

**Bohr (1913):** electrons occupy only certain stationary orbits with quantised angular momentum $L=\dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$, in which they do not radiate; a photon of energy $hf=E_i-E_f$ is emitted or absorbed when an electron moves between levels.
*Improvement:* accounted for atomic stability and quantitatively predicted the hydrogen line spectrum (Rydberg equation).
*Limitations:* an unjustified mix of classical and quantum ideas; fails for multi-electron atoms, line intensities, fine structure and Zeeman splitting.

questions.question: The graph shows the average binding energy per nucleon for a range of nuclides. Elements to the left of Fe-56 are formed by nuclear fusion. Explain how this is related to binding energy.
questions.answer: Binding energy is the energy needed to separate a nucleus into its nucleons; binding energy per nucleon measures stability, and peaks near iron-56. When light nuclei fuse into a heavier nucleus closer to the peak, the product has greater binding energy per nucleon than the reactants. The products have less mass, and the difference is released as energy, so fusion is energetically favourable up to about iron.

questions.question: A uranium-235 nucleus will break into two smaller nuclei if it captures a neutron. What is this process called?
questions.answer: Nuclear fission.

questions.question: For example, ${}^{1}_{0}n+{}^{235}_{92}U\rightarrow{}^{141}_{56}Ba+{}^{92}_{36}Kr+3\,{}^{1}_{0}n$, releasing energy. Where does the energy come from and how could it be calculated?
questions.answer: The total mass of the products is less than that of the reactants; the mass defect is converted to energy. Calculate $\Delta m=m_{reactants}-m_{products}$ and use $E=\Delta mc^2$ (or $931.5$ MeV per atomic mass unit).

questions.question: Muons are unstable particles that decay with a mean lifetime of 2.2 μs. They are produced when cosmic rays strike the upper atmosphere about 11.4 km above Earth's surface and travel very close to the speed of light relative to Earth. Explain how observations of these muons support Einstein's special theory of relativity.
questions.answer:
Classically a muon would travel only about $vt=3\times10^8\times2.2\times10^{-6}=660$ m in its mean lifetime, so very few should survive 11.4 km. In fact large numbers are detected at the surface.
- **Earth frame:** the moving muons' clocks run slow (time dilation, $t=\gamma t_0$), so they live long enough to reach the ground.
- **Muon frame:** its lifetime is 2.2 μs, but the atmosphere moving towards it is length-contracted ($l=l_0/\gamma$), so the distance is short enough to cross.
The observed numbers agree with these predictions, confirming special relativity.

questions.question: Technetium-99m, produced at the ANSTO reactor, has a decay constant of $3.2\times10^{-5}$ s$^{-1}$. What is its half-life in hours?
questions.answer: $$t_{1/2}=\frac{\ln2}{\lambda}=\frac{0.693}{3.2\times10^{-5}}=2.17\times10^4\text{ s}\approx6.0\text{ h}$$

questions.question: Technetium-99m is a pure gamma emitter. The activities of two samples were measured with a Geiger counter under the same conditions, and one was three times the other. What does this tell you about the two samples?
questions.answer: Activity $A=\lambda N$ and $\lambda$ is the same for both, so the more active sample contains three times as many undecayed Tc-99m nuclei (three times the mass of Tc-99m).

questions.question: Technetium-99m is formed from the decay of molybdenum-99. What type of particle does molybdenum-99 emit to form technetium-99m?
questions.answer: A beta-minus particle (electron), with an antineutrino: ${}^{99}_{42}Mo\rightarrow{}^{99m}_{43}Tc+{}^{0}_{-1}e+\bar\nu$.

questions.question: The graph shows how the number of molybdenum-99 nuclei changes over time as they decay. What is the half-life of molybdenum-99 in days?
questions.answer: Reading the time for the number to fall from 100 000 to 50 000 gives about 2.7 days.

questions.question: The graph shows how the number of molybdenum-99 nuclei changes over time as they decay. What percentage of the original molybdenum-99 remains after 8 days?
questions.answer: From the graph about 13 000 of the original 100 000 remain at 8 days, i.e. about 13% (check: $(\tfrac12)^{8/2.7}\approx0.13$).
